author: stacy-jankowski
description: An awkward remark, a compliment: either way, your cheeks heat up and turn pink. What the body is doing at that moment, and why there is almost nothing you can do about it.

hero.hook: One clumsy remark and your cheeks catch fire. A compliment, and the same thing happens. Nobody decides to blush.

blocks.text: Everyone knows the feeling. Someone makes an embarrassing remark about you: your face heats up, your skin turns pink. The phenomenon intrigued even the naturalist [[Charles Darwin]], who saw in it "the most peculiar and most human of all expressions."

The strangest part is that a compliment produces the same effect as mockery. Praised in front of others, you feel the same warmth rise to your cheeks. What exactly is happening under the skin, and why does the body respond the same way to shame and to pleasure?

Blushing is first of all a matter of blood. The volume flowing through the small vessels of the face, which lie very close to the surface of the skin, suddenly increases. This is controlled by the [[sympathetic nervous system]], the branch of the nervous system that runs the [[fight-or-flight response]], our emergency reaction to danger.

blocks.caption: Figures seen through a thermal imaging camera: the hotter a surface, the brighter it shows on the screen.

blocks.text: When this system switches on, the heart beats faster and body temperature climbs. To shed the excess heat, the vessels of the face dilate: more blood flows through them, and the heat it carries escapes through the skin. Because those vessels lie so close to the surface, the rush is visible: the skin turns pink or red. Blushing is a cooling system at work.

sections.title: A rush of heat under the skin

blocks.text: A social blunder, an unwritten rule broken without meaning to: the brain treats it as a threat. It activates the sympathetic nervous system, with the urge to defend yourself ("fight") or to disappear ("flight"). Blood rushes into the vessels of the face, and the cheeks flare up.

blocks.caption: Hiding your face behind your hands: the everyday version of the flight reflex.

blocks.text: Some people blush much more than others. Those who suffer from [[social anxiety]] often judge themselves harshly, whatever they do. This negative bias amplifies the response of the sympathetic system, and the slightest slip sets off a full-blown alarm throughout the body.

Fear of blushing makes you blush. In people who dread their own redness, simply being aware of being watched strengthens the sympathetic response. So you blush because you blushed, and the loop closes.

Positive attention triggers the same mechanism. Public praise, applause, an unexpected compliment: you suddenly feel exposed to other people's eyes, or worried about not knowing how to say thank you properly. That discomfort is enough to set off the emergency response.

blocks.caption: The mayor of Boston applauds a speaker at an outdoor luncheon in the 1960s: positive attention makes you blush too.

blocks.text: The brain, for its part, can tell a compliment from a humiliation perfectly well. But the sympathetic nervous system is cruder: it has not yet decided whether you need to run away. By the time it makes up its mind, your face has already changed color.

Not really, and that is fine: blushing is a natural response to the social world around us, not a flaw to be corrected. What you can work on is the trigger, that is, the way the brain files an embarrassing situation under "danger."

Two approaches can help. One is [[exposure therapy]], which means facing feared situations step by step, until they no longer set off the alarm. The other is [[mindfulness]], which teaches you to observe the rising heat without dreading it. In both cases, the blushing is not removed: the fear of blushing is defused, and the loop quiets down.

Blushing is the sympathetic nervous system dilating the vessels of the face to shed the heat of an alert, whether it comes from a blunder or a compliment: you cannot stop it, but you can learn to stop fearing it.
